title: Pass by value: what that means in Go

videos.script: Lesson 21 ended with closures, functions that keep hold of a variable. This lesson asks what a function gets when you call it. In Go the answer is short. It always gets a copy. {{copy}} Pass an int and the function has an int of its own. Pass a struct and it has its own struct, every field of it. Change it inside, and the caller never sees. {{headers}} Then the types that seem to break the rule. A function can add keys to a map, and the caller sees them. So people say Go passes maps by reference. It does not. A map value is a small thing holding a pointer, and the pointer is what gets copied. One assignment inside a function proves it. {{cost}} Last, the price. Copying sixteen bytes costs next to nothing. Copying eight megabytes does not, and you will time both from an ordinary program. By the end you can look at any parameter and say what the function can change, and what it cannot.
